## Appendix B Measuring the quality of noisy encoded computations

Measuring the quality of encoded computations in the absence of full error correction is nontrivial, because physical errors affect encoded qubits quite differently compared to physical qubits. In this section, we take some initial steps towards a theory of logical gate fidelities (Section B.2). Before we do so, we recap the basics of stabilizer codes and analyze the effective noise channels arising on the logical qubits (Section B.1).

### B.1 Stabilizer codes and logical noise channels

Let $S$ be an abelian subgroup of the Pauli group such that $-\mathbbm{1}\notin S$ . The size of $S$ is $2^{n-k}$ for an integer $k$ . The code space projector

$$ \Pi_{0}=\frac{1}{2^{n-k}}\sum_{g\in S}g, $$

defines an $[\![n,k,d]\!]$ quantum error correcting code where $d$ is the code distance. Taking a minimal size generating set for $S=\langle g_{1},\ldots,g_{n-k}\rangle$ , we can re-express $\Pi=\prod_{i=1}^{n-k}(\mathbbm{1}+g_{i})/2$ .

For two Pauli operators $P$ and $Q$ , define the scalar commutator as $[[P,Q]]=0\in\mathbb{F}_{2}$ if $[P,Q]=0$ and $[[P,Q]]=1\in\mathbb{F}_{2}$ if $PQ=-QP$ . We can define a canonical basis for the Pauli group with reference to our generating set for $S$ as follows: find a set of operators $\{h_{1},\ldots,h_{n-k}\}$ called destabilizers [142] that satisfy $[[h_{i},h_{j}]]=0$ and $[[g_{i},h_{j}]]=\delta_{ij}$ , as well as a set of logical operators $\{\bar{X}_{1},\bar{Z}_{1},\ldots,\bar{X}_{k},\bar{Z}_{k}\}$ that satisfy $[[\bar{X}_{i},h_{j}]]=[[\bar{X}_{i},g_{j}]]=[[\bar{X}_{i},\bar{X}_{j}]]=0$ , $[[\bar{Z}_{i},h_{j}]]=[[\bar{Z}_{i},g_{j}]]=[[\bar{Z}_{i},\bar{Z}_{j}]]=0$ , and $[[\bar{X}_{i},\bar{Z}_{j}]]=\delta_{ij}$ . This canonical basis set can be found efficiently by solving a set of linear equations over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ .

A logical state $\ket{\bar{\psi}}$ is any state that satisfies $\Pi_{0}\ket{\bar{\psi}}=g\ket{\bar{\psi}}=\ket{\bar{\psi}}$ for all $g\in S$ . A syndrome is a set of measurement outcomes $s\in\{0,1\}^{n-k}$ for the stabilizer generators $g_{i}$ . The projector onto a given syndrome outcome is

$$ \Pi_{s}=\prod_{i=1}^{n-k}\frac{\mathbbm{1}+(-1)^{s_{i}}g_{i}}{2}. $$

We also define $\Pi_{0r}$ as the projector onto the $r$ -error subspace

$$ \mathrm{span}\Big(\{P\ket{\bar{\psi}}:\Pi_{0}\ket{\bar{\psi}}=\ket{\bar{\psi}},\,P\in P_{n},\,\mathrm{wt}(P)\leq r\}\Big), $$

where $P=\bigotimes_{i=1}^{n}P_{i}$ is a Pauli operator and $\mathrm{wt}(P)=|\{i:P_{i}\neq\mathbbm{1}\}$ is the weight of $P$ , i.e., the number of non-identity Paulis in $P$ . The projector $\Pi_{0r}$ can be interpreted as a projector onto the set of states that have at most $r$ errors. Note, $\Pi_{0n}=\mathbbm{1}$ , while the smallest $m$ such that $\Pi_{0m}=\mathbbm{1}$ is greater than or equal to the code distance, but will generally depend on the code.

In order to formalize the effect of physical noise on the logical subspace it is convenient to introduce a generalization of a quantum channel, called quantum instrument.

#### Definition 15.

A quantum instrument is a collection of CP maps $\{\mathcal{E}_{a}\}_{a\in A}$ such that $\sum_{a\in A}\mathcal{E}_{a}$ is a quantum channel.

A projective measurement $\{\Pi_{a}\}_{a\in M}$ is an example of a quantum instrument, where $a$ indexes the possible measurement outcomes $M$ .

For a given physical noise channel $\mathcal{E}$ , the corresponding logical noise channel is the quantum instrument $\{\mathcal{E}_{s}\}_{s\in\{0,1\}^{n-k}}$ associated with the syndrome outcomes

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{s}(\rho) \displaystyle=\Pi_{s}\mathcal{E}(\rho)\Pi_{s}=\sum_{\mu}\Pi_{s}K_{\mu}\rho K_{\mu}^{\dagger}\Pi_{s}. $$

For an initial state in the code space, these are effectively logical channels with the Kraus operators

$$ \displaystyle\Pi_{s}K_{\mu}\Pi_{0} \displaystyle=h^{s}\Pi_{0}h^{s}K_{\mu}\Pi_{0}=\sum_{abc}c_{abcs}^{\mu}h^{s}g^{c}\bar{X}^{b}\bar{Z}^{a}\Pi_{0}, $$

where $h^{s}\equiv\prod_{i=1}^{n-k}h_{i}^{s_{i}}$ is a product of destabilizers that corrects the syndrome and $c_{abcs}^{\mu}=\mathrm{Tr}[K_{\mu}\bar{Z}^{a}\bar{X}^{b}g^{c}h^{s}]$ .

### B.2 Logical gate fidelities

We are now ready to define notions of logical transversal gate fidelities. Due to entanglement that builds up between syndrome degrees of freedom and logical degrees of freedom during the computation, the error model for logical qubits is intrinsically non-Markovian, increasing the relative importance of circuit context dependence in defining gate fidelities. We provide a partial resolution to this challenge through the use of $r$ -error filters that restrict the input states of the logical channel to have at most weight- $r$ errors.

Given a syndrome outcome $s$ , a decoder is a map from $s$ to a logical Pauli operator $\bar{P}_{s}$ chosen to correct the error and a destabilizer $\bar{h}^{s}$ that fixes the syndrome without affecting the logical degrees of freedom. We define the $(r,s)$ -filtered average gate fidelity of a decoded logical operation $\bar{\mathcal{U}}=\bar{U}\cdot\bar{U}^{\dagger}$ conditioned on a particular syndrome outcome $s$ acting on an $r$ -error state as

$$ \displaystyle F_{sr}(\mathcal{E},\bar{\mathcal{U}}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{p_{sr}}\int d\psi_{r}\bra{\psi_r}\bar{U}^{\dagger}\bar{P}_{s}h^{s} \displaystyle\times\mathcal{E}_{s}(\bar{U}\ket{\psi_r}\bra{\psi_r}\bar{U}^{\dagger})h^{s}\bar{P}_{s}U\ket{\psi_r}, \displaystyle p_{sr} \displaystyle=\mathrm{Tr}[\mathcal{E}_{s}(\Pi_{0r}/d_{r})], \displaystyle d_{r} \displaystyle=\mathrm{Tr}[\Pi_{0r}], $$

where $\mathcal{E}\circ\bar{\mathcal{U}}(\rho)$ is the noisy implementation of the logical gate $\bar{\mathcal{U}}$ , $h^{s}$ maps the states with syndrome $s$ back to the logical states, $d\psi_{r}$ is the uniform measure on the set of $r$ -error states induced by the Haar measure over logical operators and $p_{sr}$ is the probability of observing syndrome $s$ starting from a maximally mixed state in the $r$ -error space. In the case of error detection, where the optimal decoding strategy is to postselect on the all- $0$ syndrome outcome and set $\bar{P}_{0}=\mathbbm{1}$ , the average gate fidelity is

$$ F_{0r}(\mathcal{E},\bar{\mathcal{U}})=\frac{1}{p_{0r}}\int d\psi_{r}\bra{\psi_r}\bar{U}^{\dagger}\mathcal{E}_{0}(\bar{U}\ket{\psi_r}\bra{\psi_r}\bar{U}^{\dagger})U\ket{\psi_r}. $$

In addition to the average gate fidelity, we also introduce the $(r,s)$ -filtered entanglement fidelity [143, 144]

$$ F_{esr}(\mathcal{E},\bar{\mathcal{U}})=\frac{1}{p_{sr}}\bra{\Phi_r}(\mathcal{U}^{{\dagger}}\circ\mathcal{R}_{s}\circ\mathcal{E}_{s}\circ\mathcal{U})\otimes\mathbbm{1}(\ket{\Phi_r}\bra{\Phi_r})\ket{\Phi_r}, $$

where $\mathcal{R}_{s}(\rho)=\bar{P}_{s}h^{s}\rho h^{s}\bar{P}_{s}$ and $\ket{\Phi_r}=\operatorname{vec}(\Pi_{0r}/d_{r})$ is a purification of the density matrix $\Pi_{0r}/d_{r}$ . As with their standard versions, we find that the $(r,s)$ -filtered entanglement fidelity is related to the $(r,s)$ -filtered average gate fidelity through the formula [145, 146]

$$ F_{sr}=\frac{d_{r}F_{esr}+1}{d_{r}+1}. $$

To see this equality, one follows the simple proof of Nielsen [146]. Similarly, we can use the $r$ -filtered average gate fidelity to upper- and lower-bound an $(r,s)$ -filtered version of the diamond distance (defined analogously with respect to $r$ -error input states and decoding conditioned on syndrome outcome $s$ ) of the logical channel from the identity [e.g. 147, Prop. 9].

We can analytically compute the $(r,s)$ -filtered entanglement fidelity as

$$ \displaystyle F_{esr} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{p_{sr}d_{r}^{2}}\sum_{\mu}\left\lvert\mathrm{Tr}\big[\Pi_{0}\bar{P}_{s}h^{s}K_{\mu}\Pi_{0r}\big]\right\lvert^{2}, $$

where $\{K_{\mu}\}$ are a set of Kraus operators for $\mathcal{E}$ . For two-qubit logical gates between code blocks (e.g., the transversal CNOT) and two-qubit gate error channels that factorize $\mathcal{E}=\mathcal{E}_{1}\otimes\mathcal{E}_{2}$ , we can directly extend this formula to two-qubit logical gates

$$ F_{ess^{\prime}rr^{\prime}}=F_{esr}^{(1)}F_{es^{\prime}r^{\prime}}^{(2)}. $$

These definitions of logical gate fidelities implicitly assume either that $r$ is less than the code distance or that most states in the $r$ -error space are close to a logical state. Otherwise, the $r$ -filtered gate fidelity is dominated by the projection back to the code space. In the case of near-term experiments where accessible code distances are small, which is the focus of this work, it is convenient to define an intermediate notion of logical fidelity that looks at the fidelity of the logical operation on the whole $r$ -error space without error correction and decoding following the gate. The error rate of this fidelity does not decrease with increasing code distance, but provides a useful bound on the fidelity of logical gates in a near-term logical circuit. We thus define the $r$ -filtered average gate fidelity and $r$ -filtered entanglement fidelity as

$$ \displaystyle F_{r}(\mathcal{E},\bar{\mathcal{U}}) \displaystyle=\frac{d_{r}F_{er}(\mathcal{E},\bar{\mathcal{U}})+1}{d_{r}+1}, \displaystyle F_{er}(\mathcal{E},\bar{\mathcal{U}}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{p_{r}}\bra{\Phi_r}(\bar{\mathcal{U}}^{\dagger}\circ\mathcal{E}\circ\bar{\mathcal{U}})\otimes\mathbbm{1}(\ket{\Phi_r}\bra{\Phi_r})\ket{\Phi_r}, \displaystyle p_{r} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{d_{r}}\mathrm{Tr}[\Pi_{0r}\mathcal{E}(\Pi_{0r})], $$

respectively. In the case of $[\![8,3,2]\!]$ codes, for $r=1$ , $\Pi_{01}$ has support on 144 out of all possible 256 states. For $r\geq 2$ , $\Pi_{0r}$ has support on the whole 8-qubit Hilbert space. Consequently, in this case $F_{sr}$ is negligible for any $r>0$ ; however, $F_{r}$ can still be large because of the small size of the code.

In Fig. 4(b) in the main text, we present the $r$ -filtered gate fidelities $F_{r}$ for transversal CCZ, in-block CNOT, and transversal CNOT gates of the $[\![8,3,2]\!]$ code. In the calculations for the CCZ and transversal CNOT gates we took iid depolarizing noise on each qubit following the application of a physical gate. For the in-block CNOT, which we assume to be implemented via qubit reconfiguration, we modeled the noise as pure $Z$ -dephasing noise on each qubit following the gate. To numerically compute the $r$ -filtered fidelities we directly evaluated the formulas above by expressing them as polynomials in the local noise rate parameter $p(1-p)$ . We then used direct calculations on the $2^{8}$ dimensional Hilbert space to evaluate the coefficients of each polynomial.

For a native two-qubit gate error rate of $0.5\%$ , the fidelity of a compiled CCZ gate would be around $3\%$ . We see in Fig. 4(b) that the $r$ -filtered fidelity can readily exceed that for $r\,{=}\,0$ , while at high enough single-qubit gate error rates $10^{-3}-10^{-4}$ the transversal CCZ fidelity exceeds the compiled version for $r\,{>}\,0$ . In the case of transversal CNOTs shown in Fig. 4(b), the $r$ -filtered fidelity only exceeds the native fidelity for $r\,{=}\,0$ . The pseudothreshold for two-qubit CNOT gates is observed to be at gate error rates of $4\%$ . When comparing the fidelity of physical CNOTs implemented on 3 independent pairs, which is most comparable to the logical transversal CNOT gate for the $[\![8,3,2]\!]$ code, the pseudothreshold increases to $14\%$ .

## Appendix C Model for fidelity versus acceptance fraction

As we increase the amount of postselection in the encoded circuit, the XEB improves but the number of discarded samples grows as well. In Fig. 4(a) of the main text and in the experimental data (Fig. 5(e)) of Ref. [27], the relationship between the XEB and the fraction of accepted samples reduces to a power law in a certain regime.

Here, we provide a simple model based on the $[\![8,3,2]\!]$ code that reproduces this behavior. While the exponent will differ for a different code, we expect the power-law behaviour to generalize. We consider $n$ logical qubits encoded into $n/3$ blocks of the $[\![8,3,2]\!]$ code, which experience an i.i.d. dephasing channel with rate $p$ on all physical qubits, right before measurement in the $X$ basis. For each block, we can evaluate the probability of a logical $Z$ errors conditioned on whether the single $X$ stabilizer is violated or not; this is enough to recover the power law behavior mentioned above. The probability of having $k\,{\in}\,\{0,\ldots,8\}$ errors in a block is

$$ P_{k}=\binom{8}{k}p^{k}(1-p)^{8-k}, $$

and the corresponding probability of violating the stabilizer is

$$ \epsilon=\sum_{k\in\{1,3,5,7\}}P_{k}, $$

which corresponds to having an odd number of errors. The logical operators within a block are defined up to multiplication with stabilizers, but in practice we choose a particular operator realization, e.g., the three sides of a cube highlighted in Fig. 1(d). Then, for every odd number of errors, we have a $7/8$ probability of having at least one logical fault, since for any choice of logical operators, a single physical qubit does not participate in any of them. Similarly, the probability of having a logical fault given an even number of physical errors is $\{0,1,4/5,1,0\}$ for $\{0,2,4,6,8\}$ errors, respectively. Together, this results in probabilities $p_{l}^{s}$ of logical faults conditioned on whether a stabilizer is violated ( $s=-$ ) or not ( $s=+$ ), which are given by

$$ \displaystyle p_{l}^{-} \displaystyle=7/8, \displaystyle p_{l}^{+} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{1-\epsilon}(P_{2}+\frac{4}{5}P_{4}+P_{6}). $$

Given $n_{b}=n/3$ blocks, the probability of having exactly $j$ stabilizers violated is

$$ S_{j}=\binom{n_{b}}{j}\epsilon^{j}(1-\epsilon)^{n_{b}-j}, $$

and the probability of having no logical error in that situation is

$$ F_{j}=(1-p_{l}^{-})^{j}(1-p_{l}^{+})^{n_{b}-j}. $$

The acceptance fraction for up to $m$ violated stabilizers is then

$$ \displaystyle\bar{S}_{m}=\sum_{j\leq m}S_{j}, $$

and the fidelity (i.e., the probability of no logical errors) is

$$ \displaystyle\bar{F}_{m}=\frac{1}{\bar{S}_{m}}\sum_{j\leq m}S_{j}F_{j}, $$

which results in an approximate power law (when evaluated numerically) for the fidelity $\bar{F}_{m}$ as a function of acceptance fraction $\bar{S}_{m}$ . This is in good qualitative agreement with circuit-level simulations such as those in Fig. 4(a).

Finally, we provide an analytical formula for the power-law exponent in the low-noise, highly post-selected regime. Assuming a power-law relationship $\bar{F}_{m}=a\,\bar{S}_{m}^{\alpha}$ , we can estimate $\alpha$ in the post-selected regime from $\bar{F}_{1}/\bar{F}_{0}$ and $\bar{S}_{1}/\bar{S}_{0}$ using Eqs. 68 and 69. To first order in $p$ , these are given by

$$ \displaystyle\bar{F}_{1}/\bar{F}_{0} \displaystyle=1-7n_{b}\,p+O(p^{2}), \displaystyle\bar{S}_{1}/\bar{S}_{0} \displaystyle=1+8n_{b}\,p+O(p^{2}), $$

which gives $\alpha=-7/8$ and is, to first order, independent of both $p$ and $n_{b}$ . In Fig. 4(a), we show a power law fit with this value of $\alpha$ , and observe good agreement with simulated data.

## Appendix D Statistical model for second moment quantities of IQP circuits

To characterize random circuits in terms of their output distributions in the noiseless case and their quality of implementation in the presence of noise, it is useful to analyze their second-moment quantities. Second-moment quantities include all quantites which can be expressed as average quantities that are linear in two tensor copies of the random circuits applied to a fixed initial state. Most importantly for us, the average collision probability, the cross-entropy benchmark, the average fidelity and the average purity are all second-moment quantities. In this work, we are interested in those quantities for random degree-3 IQP circuits.

In this section, we derive a framework for analysing the second-moment properties of ideal and noisy circuits with some random IQP degree- $2$ gates whose output is a polynomial binary phase state

$$ \displaystyle\ket{\psi}=\sum_{x}(-1)^{f(x)}\ket{x}, $$

for some degree- $2$ Boolean polynomial $f$ . This is simpler than analyzing degree- $3$ circuits directly, and will allow us to make statements about random degree- $3$ circuits as well, since we can fix the degree- $3$ part of a circuit and then average over its degree- $2$ part.

Importantly, our framework will not require the IQP circuits to be globally random but only locally random. Specifically, we consider circuit architectures, in which the first layer is a layer of Hadamard gates, on certain pairs $(i,j)$ of qubits, a random degree- $2$ IQP circuit $Z_{i}^{u}Z_{j}^{v}CZ_{ij}^{w}$ for $u,v,w\in\{0,1\}$ is applied. All other components of the (ideal) circuit are arbitrary gates which map binary phase states to binary phase states. We also allow for noise which preserves binary phase states.

Choose an IQP circuit $D\sim\mathfrak{I}$ from some IQP ensemble $\mathfrak{I}$ satisfying the properties above. Let us then write $\rho_{D}(\mathcal{N})$ for the mixture of binary phase states generated by $D$ with noise specified by $\mathcal{N}$ . The ideal state is given by $\rho_{D}(\{\mathbbm{1}\})=D\ket{0}\bra{0}_{x}D$ . Our central quantity of interest is now the second-moment operator

$$ \displaystyle M_{2}(\mathcal{N},\mathcal{N}^{\prime})=\mathbb{E}_{D\sim\mathfrak{I}}\left[\rho_{D}(\mathcal{N}^{\prime}),\rho_{D}(\mathcal{N})\right]. $$

To be most general, we allow different types of noise on the two copies.

The average collision probability $\overline{C}$ , average XEB fidelity $\overline{\chi}$ , average fidelity $\overline{F}$ , and average purity $\overline{P}$ can be written in terms of Eq. 73 as

$$ \displaystyle\overline{C} \displaystyle=\tr[\mathbb{X}_{x}^{\otimes n}M_{2}(\{\mathbbm{1}\},\{\mathbbm{1}\})] \displaystyle\overline{\chi} \displaystyle=2^{n}\tr[\mathbb{X}_{x}^{\otimes n}M_{2}(\{\mathbbm{1}\},\mathcal{N})]-1 \displaystyle\overline{F} \displaystyle=\tr[\mathbb{S}^{\otimes n}M_{2}(\{\mathbbm{1}\},\mathcal{N})] \displaystyle\overline{P} \displaystyle=\tr[\mathbb{S}^{\otimes n}M_{2}(\mathcal{N},\mathcal{N})] $$

where we have defined $\mathbb{S}=\sum_{x,y\in\{0,1\}}\ket{xy}_{a}\bra{yx}_{a}$ as the single-qubit swap operator between the two copies, and $\mathbb{X}_{a}=\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}}\ket{xx}_{a}\bra{xx}_{a}$ as the single-qubit ‘delta projector’ in the $a$ -basis for $a\in\{x,z\}$ . Note that while the collision probability involves no noise on either copy in $M_{2}$ , the average fidelity and average XEB fidelity involve noise on one copy and no noise on the other copy. In contrast, the purity involves noise on both copies.

Let us now derive the formalism. To start out, we consider $D$ chosen uniformly at random from degree-2 IQP circuits. As discussed in Section A.1, each such circuit is characterized by a degree- $2$ polynomial $f(x)=\sum_{ij}b_{ij}x_{i}x_{j}+\sum_{i}a_{i}x_{i}$ with uniformly random choices of $a\in\{0,1\}^{n},b\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}$ specifying the locations of the $Z$ and $CZ$ gates.

### D.1 The global second moment

In order to compute $M_{2}(\{\mathbbm{1}\},\{\mathbbm{1}\})$ we build on the proof of anticoncentration of globally random degree- $2$ IQP circuits by Bremner et al. [24] (Lemma 11 in App. F). Let $\mathfrak{I}_{n}$ be the family of uniformly random degree-2 IQP circuits on $n$ qubits, and $\mathbb{P}=\sum_{xy\in\{0,1\}}\ket{xx}\bra{yy}$ the unnormalized Bell state projector.

#### Lemma 16 (Global projector).

Consider the moment operator $M_{2}$ for random degree- $2$ IQP circuits in $\mathfrak{I}_{n}$ . It holds that

$$ \displaystyle M_{2}(\{\mathbbm{1}\},\{\mathbbm{1}\})=\frac{1}{2^{2n}}(\mathbbm{1}^{\otimes n}+\mathbb{S}^{\otimes n}+\mathbb{P}^{\otimes n}-2\mathbb{X}_{z}^{\otimes n}). $$

Before we prove the Lemma, we would like to observe the analogy with the second moment operator of the Haar measure, which is given by

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{U\sim U(d)}U^{\otimes 2}\ket{0}\bra{0}(U^{\dagger})^{\otimes 2}=\frac{1}{2d_{[2]}}(\mathbbm{1}^{\otimes n}+\mathbb{S}^{\otimes n}), $$

where $d_{[2]}$ is the dimension of the symmetric subspace of two $d$ -dimensional systems. While the diagonal action of the full unitary group is only invariant under a global swap of the two copies, giving rise to the swap operator in the moment formula (79), the diagonal action of random IQP circuits on binary phase states has additional invariances, namely, precisely those captured by the $\mathbb{P}$ and $\mathbb{X}_{z}$ operators.

#### Proof.

To show Lemma 16, we expand

$$ \displaystyle M_{2}(\{\mathbbm{1}\},\{\mathbbm{1}\})=\frac{1}{2^{2n}}\sum_{z_{1},\ldots,z_{4}}\mathbb{E}_{f}\left[(-1)^{\sum_{i}f(z_{i})}\right]\ket{z_1 z_3}\bra{z_2z_4}_{z}, $$

and observe that

$$ \mathbb{E}_{f}\left[(-1)^{\sum_{i}f(z_{i})}\right]\\
\propto\sum_{a\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\sum_{b\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}}(-1)^{\sum_{i}\left(\sum_{kl}b_{kl}z_{ik}z_{il}+\sum_{k}a_{k}z_{ik}\right)}. $$

Now, we find criteria on the $z_{i}$ that have to be satisfied for the coefficient (81) to be nonzero. Following Ref. [24] this average results in three constraints on the sums,

$$ \displaystyle(\mathbbm{1})\quad \displaystyle z_{1}=z_{2}\eqqcolon x\ {\rm and}\ z_{3}=z_{4}\eqqcolon y,\quad{\rm or} \displaystyle(\mathbb{S})\quad \displaystyle z_{1}=z_{4}\eqqcolon x\ {\rm and}\ z_{2}=z_{3}\eqqcolon y,\quad{\rm or} \displaystyle(\mathbb{P})\quad \displaystyle z_{1}=z_{3}\eqqcolon x\ {\rm and}\ z_{2}=z_{4}\eqqcolon y. $$

For the sake of completeness, we recall the derivation here. Consider the $k$ -th bits $z_{1k},z_{2k},z_{3k},z_{4k}$ of the vectors $z_{i}$ . Then any nonzero term in the exponent will result in the sum to vanish.

Hence, the sum over $a_{k}$ combined with the linear term $\sum_{k}a_{k}z_{ik}$ enforces $z_{1k}=z_{2k}+z_{3k}+z_{4k}$ . Substituting this, the sum over $b_{kl}$ now enforces that

$$ \begin{split}0&=z_{1k}z_{1l}+z_{2k}z_{2l}+z_{3k}z_{3l}+z_{4k}z_{4l}\\
&=(z_{2k}+z_{3k}+z_{4k})(z_{2l}+z_{3l}+z_{4l})\\
&+z_{2k}z_{2l}+z_{3k}z_{3l}+z_{4k}z_{4l}\\
&=z_{2k}(z_{3l}+z_{4l})+z_{3k}(z_{2l}+z_{4l})+z_{4k}(z_{2l}+z_{3l}),\end{split} $$

where we removed terms that appeared an even number of times ( $z_{2k}z_{2l}$ etc.) since they evaluate to $0$ . From the pigeonhole principle, we know that at least two of the $\{z_{2k},z_{3k},z_{4k}\}$ must be the same.

To show constraint $(\mathbbm{1})$ , choose $z_{3k}\,{=}\,z_{4k}\,{=}\,y_{k}$ and rewrite the above condition as,

$$ \displaystyle(z_{2k}+y_{k})(z_{3l}+z_{4l})=0, $$

where we again removed the term $2z_{2l}y_{k}$ . There are now two cases. In the first case, if $z_{2k}\,{\neq}\,y_{k}$ we immediately obtain $z_{3l}\,{=}\,z_{4l}$ for all $l$ and thus $z_{3}\,{=}\,z_{4}$ and $z_{1}\,{=}\,z_{2}$ . Otherwise, if $z_{2k}\,{=}\,y_{k}$ , then we have $z_{1k}\,{=}\,z_{2k}\,{=}\,z_{3k}\,{=}\,z_{4k}$ which is covered by all of the conditions in Eq. 82. The equality constraint $z_{1l}\,{=}\,z_{2l}\,{=}\,z_{3l}\,{=}\,z_{4l}$ then enforces one of the conditions in Eq. 82 on the $l$ -th bit. If the $z_{il}$ are not all equal, we can apply the first case to obtain one of the conditions in Eq. 82 for all bits. Constraints $(\mathbb{S})$ and $(\mathbb{P})$ follow from the same argument starting with the choice $z_{2k}=z_{3k}$ and $z_{2k}=z_{4k}$ , respectively.

The only overlap between the conditions is when

$$ \displaystyle(\mathbb{X}_{z})\quad z_{1}\,{=}\,z_{2}\,{=}\,z_{3}\,{=}\,z_{4}\,{=}\,x. $$

Thus, we can evaluate these three conditions independently and then subtract the over-counted terms corresponding to all four bitstrings being equal.

Each of the conditions $(\mathbbm{1}),(\mathbb{S}),(\mathbb{P}),(\mathbb{X}_{z})$ in Eqs. (82) and (84) results in the averaged exponents in Eq. 81 to be trivially even-valued, since every term will appear in pairs. Thus, the average coefficient evaluates to $1$ . The statement of the lemma follows from inserting the conditions in Eq. 80. ∎

Lemma 16 directly implies the anticoncentration lemma of Bremner et al. [24].

#### Corollary 17 (Anticoncentration of random IQP).

The average collision probability of random degree-2 IQP circuits is given by $3\cdot 2^{-n}-2^{-2n+1}$ .

#### Proof.

We apply Lemma 16 to Eq. 74 to find

$$ \displaystyle\overline{C} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2^{2n}}\tr[\mathbb{X}_{x}^{\otimes n}(\mathbbm{1}^{\otimes n}+\mathbb{S}^{\otimes n}+\mathbb{P}^{\otimes n}-2\mathbb{X}_{z}^{\otimes n})] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2^{2n}}(2^{n}+2^{n}+2^{n}-2)=3\cdot 2^{-n}-2^{-2n+1}, $$

where we have used that $\tr[\mathbb{X}_{x}\mathbb{O}]=\tr[\mathbb{X}_{z}\mathbb{O}]$ for $\mathbb{O}=\mathbbm{1},\mathbb{S},\mathbb{P}$ since the Hadamards cancel, and $\tr[\mathbb{X}_{z}\mathbb{X}_{x}]=1$ . ∎

### D.2 Statistical mechanics model for locally random degree-2 circuits

In the following, we will use the properties of IQP circuits with locally restricted random degree-2 parts. To this end, we follow a line of thought developed in Refs. [40, 36, 22]. There, the observation is, that layers of single-qubit Haar-random gates in the circuit project the corresponding second-moment operator locally onto the space spanned by the $\mathbbm{1}$ and $\mathbb{S}$ operators. The effect of any gate between those layers of single-qubit Haar-random gates can thus be projected onto this space. As it turns out, the update rules of the $\mathbbm{1}$ and $\mathbb{S}$ operators under such two-qubit gates are quite simple.

We will proceed to derive an analogous model that lets us analyze the second-moment properties of noisy and noiseless IQP circuits with certain non-random gates. The relevant state space, in the most general case, is locally spanned by the invariant subspaces of those random IQP circuits.

#### Lemma 18 (IQP invariants).

Let $O=\sum_{x,y,z,w=0}^{2^{n}-1}q(x,y,z,w)\ket{xy}\bra{zw}$ be an operator on two copies of $n$ qubits. Then

$$ \mathbb{E}_{D\sim\mathfrak{I}_{n}}[D^{\otimes 2}OD^{\otimes 2}]\\
=\sum_{x\neq y=0}^{2^{n}-1}\big[q(x,y,x,y)\ket{xy}\bra{xy}+q(x,y,y,x)\ket{xy}\bra{yx}\\
+q(x,x,y,y)\ket{xx}\bra{yy}\big]+\sum_{x=0}^{2^{n}-1}q(x,x,x,x)\ket{xx}\bra{xx}. $$

#### Proof.

We follow the same argument as in the proof of Lemma 16. ∎

Lemma 18 implies that there are $3\cdot(2^{2n}-2^{n})+2^{n}$ linearly independent operators $\ket{xy}\bra{xy},\ket{xy}\bra{yx},\ket{xx}\bra{yy}$ for all $x,y\in\{0,1\}^{n}$ which are invariant under the average over random IQP circuits. The IQP-average projects an input operator $O$ onto the space spanned by these operators.

However, for the circuits that we will be interested in, we can significantly reduce this number. To this end, we consider circuits in which there are layers of minimal units of random IQP circuits on two qubits interleaved with other, non-random gates. This is a toy model of the hIQP circuits, where we apply layers of random IQP circuits on blocks of three qubits interleaved with layers of CNOT gates.

From Lemma 18, it follows that there are $3\cdot(16-4)+4=40$ linearly independent operators on the two qubits. We reduce this number to $16$ operators which are written as arbitrary products of $4$ linearly independent operators per qubit, exploiting that our circuits are quite restrictive.

Specifically, we consider the mutually orthogonal operators on two copies of a single qubit

$$ \displaystyle{\sf I} \displaystyle=\mathbbm{1}-\mathbb{X}_{z} \displaystyle=\ket{01}\bra{01}+\ket{10}\bra{10} \displaystyle{\sf S} \displaystyle=\mathbb{S}-\mathbb{X}_{z} \displaystyle=\ket{01}\bra{10}+\ket{10}\bra{01} \displaystyle{\sf P} \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}-\mathbb{X}_{z} \displaystyle=\ket{00}\bra{11}+\ket{11}\bra{00} \displaystyle{\sf X} \displaystyle=\mathbb{X}_{z} \displaystyle=\ket{00}\bra{00}+\ket{11}\bra{11}. $$

We define the local state space to be $\mathcal{S}=\{{\sf I},{\sf S},{\sf P},{\sf X}\}$ . It will also be useful to define $\mathcal{S}_{\neg{\sf X}}=\mathcal{S}\setminus\{{\sf X}\}$ . The operators ${\sf I},{\sf S},{\sf P},{\sf X}$ directly correspond to mutually exclusive constraints $({\sf I}),({\sf S}),({\sf P}),({\sf X})$ analogous to the (non-exclusive) constraints $(\mathbbm{1}),(\mathbb{S}),(\mathbb{P}),(\mathbb{X}_{z})$ defined in Eqs. 82 and 84.

The circuit components we now need to analyze are

- 1. state preparation of $\ket{+^n}\bra{+^n}^{\otimes 2}$ ,

- 2. layers of random IQP circuits $\prod_{i=1}^{n/2}D_{2i,2i+1}^{\otimes 2}$ , where $D_{2i,2i+1}\in\mathfrak{I}_{2}$ are random degree- $2$ IQP circuits on two qubits,

- 3. $\mathrm{CNOT}_{i,j}^{\otimes 2}$ gates between any two sites $i$ and $j$ ,

- 4. $X$ and $Z$ noise, that is operators $X\otimes\mathbbm{1}$ , $Z\otimes\mathbbm{1}$ applied to the two-copy state.

Let us first consider state preparation. We find that under a $z$ -twirl the two-copy state $\ket{+^n}\bra{+^n}^{\otimes 2}$ can be expressed as

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{z\in\{0,1\}} \displaystyle(Z^{z})^{\otimes 2}\ket{+}\bra{+}^{\otimes 2}(Z^{z})^{\otimes 2} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{8}\sum_{u,v,w,x,z\in\{0,1\}}Z^{z}\ket{u}Z^{z}\ket{v}\bra{w}Z^{z}\bra{x}Z^{z} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}({\sf I}+{\sf S}+{\sf P}+{\sf X})^{\otimes n}. $$

In the following analysis we will therefore always assume that the first layer of the circuit is a layer of random $Z$ gates. This is no restriction in all cases we consider since this layer can be absorbed in the random $Z$ gates throughout the circuit.

#### Lemma 19 (Projection update).

Let $Q\in\mathcal{S}$ , and $P,R\in\mathcal{S}_{\neg{\sf X}}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{D\in\mathfrak{I}_{2}}\left[D^{\otimes 2}(Q\otimes{\sf X})D^{\otimes 2}\right] \displaystyle=Q\otimes{\sf X} \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{D\in\mathfrak{I}_{2}}\left[D^{\otimes 2}({\sf X}\otimes Q)D^{\otimes 2}\right] \displaystyle={\sf X}\otimes Q \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{D\in\mathfrak{I}_{2}}\left[D^{\otimes 2}(P\otimes R)D^{\otimes 2}\right] \displaystyle=\delta_{P,R}P\otimes R, $$

where $\delta_{P,R}=1$ if $P=R$ and $0$ otherwise.

#### Proof.

The proof follows immediately from Lemma 18, observing that all operators ${\sf X}\otimes Q$ and $Q\otimes{\sf X}$ satisfy one of the constraints $({\sf I}),({\sf S}),({\sf P}),({\sf X})$ , while $P\otimes R$ for $P\neq R$ does not satisfy any. ∎

In the next step, we analyze the behaviour of the operators under CNOT operators.

#### Lemma 20 (CNOT update).

Let $P,Q\in\mathcal{S}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{CNOT}^{\otimes 2}(P\otimes Q)\mathrm{CNOT}^{\otimes 2}=P\otimes\varepsilon_{P}(Q), $$

where we define the permutation $\varepsilon_{P}:\mathcal{S}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}$ according to the following table

| $Q$ | ${\sf X}$ | ${\sf I}$ | ${\sf S}$ | ${\sf P}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\varepsilon_{{\sf X}}(Q)$ | ${\sf X}$ | ${\sf I}$ | ${\sf S}$ | ${\sf P}$ |
| $\varepsilon_{{\sf I}}(Q)$ | ${\sf I}$ | ${\sf X}$ | ${\sf P}$ | ${\sf S}$ |
| $\varepsilon_{{\sf S}}(Q)$ | ${\sf S}$ | ${\sf P}$ | ${\sf X}$ | ${\sf I}$ |
| $\varepsilon_{{\sf P}}(Q)$ | ${\sf P}$ | ${\sf S}$ | ${\sf I}$ | ${\sf X}$ |

.

Notice that for any input $Q\in\mathcal{S}_{\neg{\sf X}}$ , the permutation $\varepsilon_{Q}$ swaps $Q$ with ${\sf X}$ as well as the other two states in $\mathcal{S}$ , while $\epsilon_{{\sf X}}(Q)=Q$ . In order to prove Lemma 20, and to show the behaviour under $X$ noise, the following lemma will be convenient.

#### Lemma 21 ( $X$ updates).

Let $P\in\mathcal{S}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle(X\otimes X)P(X\otimes X)=(\mathbbm{1}\otimes\mathbbm{1})P(X\otimes X)=\varepsilon_{{\sf X}}(P) \displaystyle(\mathbbm{1}\otimes X)P(\mathbbm{1}\otimes X)=(X\otimes\mathbbm{1})P(X\otimes\mathbbm{1})=\varepsilon_{{\sf I}}(P) \displaystyle(X\otimes\mathbbm{1})P(\mathbbm{1}\otimes X)=(\mathbbm{1}\otimes X)P(X\otimes\mathbbm{1})=\varepsilon_{{\sf S}}(P) \displaystyle(X\otimes X)P(\mathbbm{1}\otimes\mathbbm{1})=(\mathbbm{1}\otimes\mathbbm{1})P(X\otimes X)=\varepsilon_{{\sf P}}(P) $$

To prove the lemma, we just expand $P$ in the computational basis.

#### Proof of Lemma 20.

Given Lemma 21, the Lemma follows immediately from expanding $P$ in the computational basis and observing that every $1$ -entry in $P$ results in an $X$ applied to the corresponding entry of $Q$ . For each $P$ , the patterns o $1$ entries in $P$ , correspond exactly to one of the cases in Eqs. 99, 100, 101 and 102. For instance, for $P\otimes Q={\sf I}\otimes Q$ , we have

$$ \mathrm{CNOT}^{\otimes 2}({\sf I}\otimes Q)\mathrm{CNOT}^{\otimes 2}\\
=\ket{01}\bra{01}(\mathbbm{1}\otimes X)P(\mathbbm{1}\otimes X)+\ket{10}\bra{10}(X\otimes\mathbbm{1})P(X\otimes\mathbbm{1})\\
=\ket{01}\bra{01}\varepsilon_{{\sf I}}(Q)+\ket{10}\bra{10}\varepsilon_{{\sf I}}(Q)={\sf I}\otimes\varepsilon_{{\sf I}}(Q), $$

and likewise for the other cases. ∎

Finally, we need to analyze noise on one copy of the second moment operator. We do so for single-qubit $X$ and $Z$ noise The case of $X$ noise follows immediately from Lemma 21. For $Z$ noise we find

#### Lemma 22 ( $Z$ noise).

We have that

$$ \displaystyle(Z\otimes\mathbbm{1})P(Z\otimes\mathbbm{1})=\begin{cases}P&\text{if }P\in\{{\sf I},{\sf X}\}\\
-P&\text{if }P\in\{{\sf S},{\sf P}\}.\end{cases} $$

The lemma follows from direct calculation in the computational basis.

One might wonder whether the states in $\mathcal{S}$ remain invariant also under Toffoli gates, since those allow implementing arbitrary permutations. However, this is not the case. To see this, consider the behaviour of the operator ${\sf X}\otimes P\otimes Q$ for any $P,Q\in\mathcal{S}$ under two-copy Toffoli gates

$$ \mathrm{TOF}^{\otimes 2}({\sf X}\otimes P\otimes Q)\mathrm{TOF}^{\otimes 2}=\\
\ket{00}\bra{00}\otimes P\otimes Q+\ket{11}\bra{11}\otimes P\otimes\varepsilon_{Q}(R), $$

which cannot be decomposed into a linear combination of operators in $\mathcal{S}^{\otimes 3}$ .

Given Lemmas 19, 20, 21 and 22, we can now identify every operator $\sigma\in\mathcal{S}^{\otimes n}$ with a classical state $\ket{\sigma}$ . The second moment of a circuit with the above components can then be written as

$$ \displaystyle\ket{M_2}=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{S}^{\otimes n}}q(\sigma)\ket{\sigma}. $$

Given the second moment $\ket{M_2}$ of a certain random circuit $D$ in terms of the states $\ket{S}$ we can deduce the properties of the same circuit with a local gate or random IQP circuits applied to certain qubits $(i,j)$ as an update $T^{E}_{ij}\ket{M_2}=\sum_{S}q^{\prime}(S)\ket{S}$ , where $T_{ij}^{E}$ just acts on the tensor copies $i$ and $j$ . We can thus analyze the second moment properties of circuits as an evolution of the distribution $q$ under the local update rules derived above. The general update rule under a single parallel circuit layer with label $l$ is then given by

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{T}(\sigma^{\prime},\sigma)=\prod_{i}N^{(i)}_{\sigma_{i}^{\prime},\sigma_{i}}\prod_{\langle i,j\rangle}T^{(ij)}_{\sigma_{i}^{\prime},\sigma_{j}^{\prime},\sigma_{i},\sigma_{j}}, $$

where the $Z$ and $X$ noise update matrices $N^{Z}$ and $N^{X}\in\{0,1\}^{4\times 4}$ are defined by the update rules (104) and (100), respectively, and the CNOT and random two-qubit IQP circuit update matrices $M^{\mathrm{CNOT}},M^{\mathfrak{I}_{2}}\in\{0,1\}^{16\times 16}$ by Lemmas 20 and 19, respectively.

In order to compute our properties of interest in Eqs. 74, 75, 76 and 77, we need to compute the overlap of the resulting state with the $\mathbb{X}_{x}$ and $\mathbb{S}$ states. Defining $\innerproduct{Q}{P}=\tr[QP]$ , we observe that

$$ \displaystyle\innerproduct{\mb S}{Q} \displaystyle=\begin{cases}2&\text{if }Q\in\{{\sf S},{\sf X}\}\\
0&\text{if }Q\in\{{\sf I},{\sf P}\}\\
\end{cases} \displaystyle\innerproduct{\Xx}{Q} \displaystyle=1\quad\forall Q\in\mathcal{S}. $$

## Appendix E Anticoncentration of degree- $D$ circuits

Using the rules derived in this section, we can analyze the second-moment properties of arbitrary noiseless circuits with some random IQP degree- $2$ parts and $X$ , CNOT gates, as well as their behaviour under single-qubit Pauli noise. To start out, let us apply the model to compute some simple quantities of which we already know.

First, we compute the fidelity of the ideal state with itself, which of course evaluates to one. We begin with the initial state $\ket{+^n}$ . We find

$$ \displaystyle\tr[\mathbb{S}^{\otimes n}M_{2}(\{\mathbbm{1}\},\{\mathbbm{1}\})]=\frac{1}{4^{n}}\sum_{Q\in\mathcal{S}^{\otimes n}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\tr[Q_{i}\mathbb{S}]. $$

But $\tr[Q_{i}\mathbb{S}]=0$ unless $Q_{i}={\sf X}$ or $Q_{i}={\sf S}$ by Eq. 108. Hence, only all products of ${\sf X}$ and ${\sf S}$ are nonzero, and evaluate equally to $2^{n}$ . But there are exactly $2^{n}$ such terms and hence

$$ \displaystyle\overline{F}=\frac{1}{4^{n}}\sum_{Q\in\mathcal{S}^{\otimes n}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\tr[Q_{i}\mathbb{S}]=\frac{1}{4^{n}}\sum_{S\in\{{\sf X},{\sf S}\}^{\otimes n}}2^{n}=1. $$

Since the states in $\{{\sf X},{\sf S}\}^{\otimes n}$ are invariant under the two-qubit IQP circuit, and swap and entangling gates just permute them, the fidelity remains unchanged under the action of a circuit.

Next, let us evaluate the XEB score. For XEB every term in $\mathcal{S}^{\otimes n}$ contributes equally with a value $1$ . For the state $\ket{+^n}$ we thus find

$$ \displaystyle\overline{\chi} \displaystyle=2^{n}\tr[M_{2}(\{\mathbbm{1}\},\{\mathbbm{1}\}){\sf X}^{\otimes n}]-1 \displaystyle=\frac{2^{n}}{4^{n}}\sum_{Q\in\mathcal{S}^{\otimes n}}\prod_{i}\tr[Q_{i}{\sf X}]-1 \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2^{n}}4^{n}-1=2^{n}-1, $$

an exponentially large value.

Applying a uniformly random IQP circuit on the to $\ket{+^n}$ , however, should reduces the XEB score to the value found in Corollary 17. To see how this score comes about in our model, we write a uniformly random $n$ -qubit IQP circuit as $n(n-1)/2$ independent random two-qubit IQP circuits $D_{(i,j)}$ on every (unordered) pair of qubits $(i,j)$ . This is equivalent to an $n$ -qubit random IQP circuit, since the Z-gates just commute to the end, yielding a uniformly random string. But every two-qubit random IQP circuit $D_{(i,j)}$ acts as a constraint on the states of the model at positions $(i,j)$ , namely, any state $S\in\mathcal{S}^{\otimes n}$ with $S_{i},S_{j}\in\mathcal{S}_{\neg{\sf X}}$ and $S_{i}\neq S_{j}$ is annihilated by the constraint. We thus find

$$ M_{2}(\{\mathbbm{1}\},\{\mathbbm{1}\})=\mathbb{E}_{\{D_{(i,j)}\}}[(\prod_{i,j}D_{(i,j)})\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}^{\otimes n}}S(\prod_{i,j}D_{(i,j)})]\\
=\sum_{S\in\{{\sf X},{\sf I}\}^{\otimes n}\cup\{{\sf X},{\sf S}\}^{\otimes n}\cup\{{\sf X},{\sf P}\}^{\otimes n}}S-2{\sf X}^{\otimes n}\\
=\mathbbm{1}^{\otimes n}+\mathbb{S}^{\otimes n}+\mathbb{P}^{\otimes n}-2\mathbb{X}_{z}^{\otimes n}, $$

which recovers the result of Lemma 19 since the sum over all elements in $\{{\sf X},{\sf S}\}^{\otimes n}$ equals $\mathbb{S}$ .

### E.1 Sparse degree-2 IQP circuits

Let us now consider the first nontrivial example, namely, the following circuit model. Consider a random IQP circuit with $\ell$ layers such that every layer is given by a random two-qubit IQP circuit $D_{(i,j)}$ on a random qubit pair $i,j$ . We would now like to derive the anticoncentration properties of those circuits as a function of $d$ .

#### Theorem 23 (Anticoncentration of sparse random IQP).

Consider random degree- $2$ IQP circuits on $n$ qubits with uniformly random $Z$ gates and random CZ gates acting on $\ell$ random pairs. Then

$$ \displaystyle\overline{\chi} \displaystyle\in 2-2^{-n+1}+p(n)2^{-2\ell/n} \displaystyle\text{if }\ell\geq\frac{11}{4}n\log(n) \displaystyle\overline{\chi} \displaystyle\in\Omega(2^{n}) \displaystyle\text{if }\ell\in O(n), $$

where $p(n)=n^{11/2}/(2\pi)^{3/2}$ .

#### Proof.

For $Q\in\mathcal{S}$ , define the $Q$ -Hamming weight of a string $S\in\mathcal{S}$ as

$$ \displaystyle n_{Q}(S)=|\{i:S_{i}=Q\}|. $$

We now observe that the action of a circuit layer on the states $\ket{S}$ depends only on the number of pairs $S_{i}\neq S_{j}$ such that $S_{i},S_{j}\in\mathcal{S}_{\neg{\sf X}}$ . Let us call a string $S$ with the property of having $k$ of such pairs a string with $PQ$ -weight $k$ , written as $\mathrm{pqw}(S)=k$ . We have that

$$ \mathrm{pqw}(S)\equiv N(n_{\sf I}(S),n_{\sf S}(S),n_{\sf P}(S))\\
\coloneqq n_{\sf I}(S)n_{\sf S}(S)+n_{\sf I}(S)n_{\sf P}(S)+n_{\sf S}(S)n_{\sf P}(S). $$

The probability that a state $S\in\mathcal{S}^{\otimes n}$ is annihilated in a single circuit layer is then given by $\mathrm{pqw}(S)/\binom{n}{2}$ since there are $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs in total.

Let us write the random circuit in layer $i$ with a random degree- $2$ circuit in a random location as $D_{i}$ . Let us also define the sets

$$ \displaystyle W_{n} \displaystyle\coloneqq\{(k,l,m)\in[n]^{\times 3}:k+l+m\leq n\} \displaystyle W_{n}^{*} \displaystyle\coloneqq W_{n}\setminus\{(k,l,m): \displaystyle\quad k=l=0\vee k=m=0\vee l=m=0\} \displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{n}^{(k,l,m)} \displaystyle\coloneqq\{S\in\mathcal{S}^{\otimes n}: \displaystyle\quad n_{\sf I}(S)=k,n_{\sf S}(S)=l,n_{\sf P}(S)=m\} $$

We now write

$$ \displaystyle\overline{\chi}+1 \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2^{n}}\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}\mathbb{E}_{\{D_{i}\}}\tr[\left(\prod_{i=1}^{\ell}D_{i}\right)S\left(\prod_{i=1}^{\ell}D_{i}\right)\mathbb{X}_{x}] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2^{n}}\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}\left(1-\frac{\mathrm{pqw}(S)}{\binom{n}{2}}\right)^{\ell} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2^{n}}\sum_{(k,l,m)\in W_{n}}|\mathcal{S}_{n}^{(k,l,m)}|\left(1-\frac{N(k,l,m)}{\binom{n}{2}}\right)^{\ell}, $$

and observe that the strings with generalized Hamming weight in $W_{n}^{*}$ contribute exactly the ideal score of $3-2^{-n+1}$ to the XEB score so that

$$ \displaystyle\overline{\chi} \displaystyle=2-\frac{2}{2^{n}}+\frac{1}{2^{n}}\sum_{(k,l,m)\in W_{n}^{*}}|\mathcal{S}_{n}^{(k,l,m)}|\left(1-\frac{N(k,l,m)}{\binom{n}{2}}\right)^{\ell}. $$

Let us now bound the terms in Eq. 126. To this end, we observe that

$$ \displaystyle|W_{n}^{*}| \displaystyle=n^{3}-3n \displaystyle|\mathcal{S}_{n}^{(k,l,m)}| \displaystyle=\binom{n}{k}\binom{n-k}{l}\binom{n-k-l}{m}. $$

Using Stirling’s formula for $k=pn$ we find the exact scaling of the binomial coefficients to be

$$ \displaystyle\binom{n}{pn}\in\left(\frac{1}{2\pi np(1-p)}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}2^{nH(p)}, $$

where $H(p)=-p\log p-(1-p)\log(1-p)$ is the binary entropy function ( $\log$ has base $2$ ). We thus find that

$$ \displaystyle\overline{\chi}-2+2^{-n+1}\leq\frac{n^{7/2}}{(2\pi)^{3/2}}\times \displaystyle\times\max_{(k,l,m)\in W_{n}^{*}}2^{-\left[n+\frac{\ell}{\binom{n}{2}}N(k,l,m)-n\left[H(\frac{k}{n})+H(\frac{l}{n})+H(\frac{m}{n})\right]\right]}. $$

Now, since $2^{-x}$ is monotonously decreasing in $x$ we want to find the minimum exponent

$$ \min_{(k,l,m)\in W_{n}^{*}}\bigg\{n+\frac{\ell}{\binom{n}{2}}N(k,l,m)\\
-n\left[H\left(\frac{k}{n}\right)+H\left(\frac{l}{n}\right)+H\left(\frac{m}{n}\right)\right]\bigg\}. $$

To show the claim, observe that the entropy function $H(p)\leq 1$ and attains this value at $p=1/2$ . This implies that $n[H(\epsilon)+H(\delta)+H(\theta)]\leq 3n$ . More generally, let $k/n=\epsilon,l/n=\delta,m/n=\theta$ for arbitrary constants $\epsilon,\delta,\theta\in(0,1)$ . For this choice, $2\ell N(k,l,m)/(n(n-1))\geq 2\ell(\epsilon\delta+\epsilon\theta+\delta\theta)$ . For sufficiently large $\ell$ we therefore have $2\ell N(\epsilon,\delta,\theta)\geq n[H(\epsilon)+H(\delta)+H(\theta)]$ for any choice of $\epsilon,\delta,\theta\in\Theta(1)$ . One might think $\ell=Cn$ for a large enough constant $C$ is sufficient, but observe that for any constant $C$ , we can find constants $\epsilon,\delta$ such that $2C\epsilon\delta<H(\epsilon)+H(\delta)$ . Thus, we need to choose $\ell/n=f(n)$ to follow an arbitrary monotonously increasing function $f(n)$ that diverges with $n$ . Otherwise, the corresponding terms in Eq. 126 will diverge exponentially, showing the claim (117).

The same argument holds if only two of $k,l,m$ are chosen proportional to $n$ , and the third one sublinear.

Let $k/n\leq 1/f(n)$ for an arbitrary montonously increasing function $f$ that diverges with $n$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle H(k/n) \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{f(n)}\log f(n)-\Big[1-\frac{1}{f(n)}\Big]\log[1-\frac{1}{f(n)}\Big] \displaystyle=-\log[1-\frac{1}{f(n)}\Big]+\frac{1}{f(n)}\log[f(n)-1] \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{f(n)}\log[f(n)]. $$

Consider $k,l,m\in o(n)$ . In this case, by the bound (132) the entropy-terms decrease as $nH(k/n)\leq no(1)$ , which is asymptotically dominated by the linearly growing term.

Now, consider $k=\Theta(n),l=m=o(n)$ —the only remaining case. Let us first fix a choice $k=n/2,l=m=1$ . In this case $H(k/n)=1$ , $H(l/n)=H(m/n)\leq\log(n)/n$ and $N(k,l,m)=n+1$ so that by the bound (132) the right hand side of Eq. 130 is at most

$$ \displaystyle p(n)2^{-2\ell/n}. $$

This bound decays for $\ell>(11/4)\cdot n\log n$ .

We can vary the parameters around the bound by increasing or decreasing $k$ , and increasing $l,m$ . Let us fix $k=n/2$ and increase $l,m>1$ . In this case, $n(H(k/n)+H(l/n)+H(m/n))\leq n+(l+m)\log(n)$ and $N(k,l,m)=(l+m)n/2+lm$ , in which case for $d>11/4$ the bound (130) decays. Next, let us decrease $k/n\leq 1/2-\epsilon$ for constant $\epsilon>0$ . Since the entropy function is symmetric about $1/2$ and $N(k,l,m)$ increases in $k$ , this is the worst case. Now, $H(k/n)\leq 1-\epsilon^{2}$ , and hence $n-nH(k/n)\geq n\epsilon^{2}$ which dominates all other terms. ∎

### E.2 Sparse degree- $D$ IQP circuits

Theorem 23 provides upper and lower bounds for sparse random degree- $2$ IQP circuits.

#### Corollary 24 (Anticoncentration of sparse degree- $D$ circuits).

Random IQP circuits with $\ell$ uniformly random degree- $2$ gates and any additional diagonal gates satisfy

$$ \displaystyle\overline{\chi}\in 2-2^{-n+1}+p(n)2^{-2\ell/n}, $$

where $p(n)=n^{11/2}/(2\pi)^{3/2}$ .

#### Proof.

The corollary follows immediately from the proof of Theorem 23, by grouping all $\ell$ random degree- $2$ gates to the beginning of the circuit. The remaining gates can only decrease the XEB since $\tr[\mathbb{X}_{x}\ket{xyzw}\bra{xyzw}]>0$ for any $x,y,z,w\in\{0,1\}$ satisfying $x+y+z+w=0$ and gates cannot generate new states. ∎
